topics.h: The rain that fell on your school today may once have been in the sea, a cloud, or even a leaf! How does water travel?
p: The Sun heats water in seas, rivers, lakes and ponds. The water slowly turns into water vapour and rises. This is evaporation.
High up in the sky, the air is cooler. Water vapour cools and turns into tiny water droplets. This is condensation. Many droplets together form clouds.
When the droplets join and become big and heavy, they fall as rain, snow or hail. This is precipitation.
Rainwater flows into rivers, lakes and seas, and some soaks into the ground. Then the cycle starts again.
Plants also give out water vapour from their leaves. This is called transpiration.

ex.q: Meena hangs wet clothes in the sun at 9 a.m. By noon they are dry. Where did the water go?
st: The Sun warmed the wet clothes.
The water in them turned into water vapour.
The vapour mixed with the air. We cannot see water vapour.
ex.a: The water evaporated into the air as water vapour.

topics.rl: Drying clothes, a puddle vanishing after rain, and drops on a cold glass of nimbu paani are all parts of the water cycle around you.

topics.h: You can live for weeks without food, but only a few days without water. Why is water so special?
p: All living things need water: people, animals and plants.
Water helps us digest food, keeps our body cool and carries waste out of the body. More than half of our body weight is water.
We use water for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, farming and in factories.
Water covers about three-fourths of the Earth's surface, but most of it is salty sea water. Only a tiny part is fresh water we can use.
We get fresh water from rain, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and from under the ground (groundwater).

ex.q: Our Earth has so much water. Why do people still say there is a shortage of water?
st: Most of Earth's water is in seas and is salty.
A lot of the fresh water is frozen as ice.
So the water we can drink is only a small part.
ex.a: Because only a very small part of Earth's water is fresh water that we can use.

topics.rl: In summer, people put out bowls of water for birds and set up 'pyaau' (free drinking water stalls) for travellers. Water is life!

topics.h: If every family in your colony saved one bucket of water a day, that would fill a whole tank in a week. Small steps make big savings!
p: We waste water when taps leak, when we leave taps running, or when we let rainwater just flow away.
Rainwater harvesting means collecting rainwater from rooftops and storing it, or sending it into the ground.
Long ago, people in India built stepwells (called baoli or vav), ponds and tanks to store water. Rani ki Vav in Gujarat is a famous stepwell.
In the desert of Rajasthan, people built covered pits called kunds or tankas to collect rainwater. Johads are small earthen dams that hold rainwater.
We can reuse water: water used to wash vegetables or rice can water the plants.

ex.q: Aarav brushes his teeth for 2 minutes with the tap running. What can he do to save water?
st: The tap does not need to run while he brushes.
He can fill a mug and use only that water.
He turns the tap off until he needs to rinse.
ex.a: Use a mug of water and keep the tap closed while brushing.

topics.rl: Many housing societies and schools in cities like Chennai and Bengaluru have rooftop rainwater harvesting. Look for pipes that carry roof water into a tank or pit!

topics.h: A river is like a traveller. It is born high in the mountains and walks hundreds of kilometres to meet the sea. Let's follow its path!
p: The place where a river begins is its source. Many Indian rivers begin at a glacier (a huge river of ice) or a spring, high in the mountains.
In the mountains, the river is narrow and flows very fast. It rolls rocks and stones along with it.
In the plains, the river becomes wider and slower. It spreads fine, rich soil called silt on its banks.
Smaller rivers that join a big river are called tributaries. The place where two rivers meet is a confluence (sangam).
The place where a river meets the sea is its mouth. Near the mouth, a river may split into many branches and drop silt to form a delta.

ex.q: Why does a river flow fast in the mountains but slowly in the plains?
st: Water always flows downhill.
In the mountains the slope is steep, so water rushes down.
In the plains the land is almost flat, so water moves slowly.
ex.a: The steep slope of the mountains makes it fast; the flat plains make it slow.

topics.rl: If you visit Rishikesh, you can see the Ganga rushing fast over stones. At Patna or Kolkata, the same river is very wide and calm.

topics.h: The Ganga begins as icy water from a glacier and ends in a delta with tigers. India's rivers have amazing stories!
p: The Ganga begins at the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand. There it is called the Bhagirathi. At Devprayag it joins the Alaknanda and is called the Ganga.
The Yamuna begins at the Yamunotri glacier. It joins the Ganga at Prayagraj. Delhi and Agra are on the banks of the Yamuna.
The Brahmaputra begins in Tibet and flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. Majuli, a huge river island, is in the Brahmaputra.
The Ganga and Brahmaputra flow into the Bay of Bengal and together form the Sundarbans delta, home of the Royal Bengal tiger.
The Narmada begins at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh and flows west into the Arabian Sea. The Godavari and Kaveri flow east into the Bay of Bengal.

ex.q: Two friends live on the banks of the same river: one in Delhi and one in Agra. Which river is it?
st: Both Delhi and Agra are in north India.
The Taj Mahal in Agra stands on the bank of the Yamuna.
Delhi is also on the Yamuna.
ex.a: The Yamuna.

topics.rl: Look at an India map: most big rivers flow east into the Bay of Bengal, but the Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.

topics.h: Long ago, people chose to live near rivers. Even today, many of our biggest cities stand on river banks. Can you guess why?
p: Rivers give water for drinking, farming, washing and cattle.
The silt spread by rivers makes the land fertile, so farmers grow rice, wheat and sugarcane in river plains.
Fishermen catch fish, and boats carry people and goods on rivers. Dams on rivers store water and make electricity.
Rivers are home to fish, turtles, crocodiles and the Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal.
Sewage, factory waste and plastic make rivers dirty. Keeping rivers clean keeps people, animals and plants healthy.

ex.q: Many towns in the past grew on river banks. Think it through: why?
st: People need water every day.
The soil near rivers is good for growing food.
Boats on rivers help in travel and trade.
ex.a: Rivers give water, fertile land for food, and a way to travel.

topics.rl: Varanasi and Patna on the Ganga, Guwahati on the Brahmaputra and Ahmedabad on the Sabarmati are cities that grew beside rivers.

topics.t: The journey of food inside us
topics.h: You eat a bite of idli. Where does it go next? It takes a long trip through a tube many metres long inside you!
p: Digestion is how our body breaks food down into tiny parts that it can use.
In the mouth, teeth cut and chew food. The tongue mixes it with saliva, which makes it soft and wet.
The food pipe carries food from the mouth to the stomach. In the stomach, digestive juices mix with the food and churn it.
In the small intestine, digestion is completed. The useful parts of food go into the blood and reach every part of the body.
The large intestine takes back water from what is left. The waste then leaves the body.

ex.q: Chew a piece of plain roti slowly for a long time. It starts to taste a little sweet. Think it through: why?
st: Roti has a lot of starch.
Saliva in the mouth starts breaking down starch.
Starch is changed into a kind of sugar, so it tastes sweet.
ex.a: Saliva starts changing the starch in roti into sugar.

topics.rl: That is why elders say 'chew your food well'. Well-chewed food is easier for the stomach and intestines to digest.

topics.h: A plate of dal, rice, sabzi and curd is like a team. Each player has a different job to keep you strong!
p: Food has nutrients, the useful parts that our body needs.
Carbohydrates and fats give us energy. Rice, roti, potato and sugar have carbohydrates. Ghee, oil, butter and nuts have fats.
Proteins help us grow and repair the body. Dal, rajma, eggs, fish, milk and paneer give us proteins.
Vitamins and minerals protect us from illness. Fruits, vegetables and milk give us these. Calcium in milk keeps bones and teeth strong.
Roughage (fibre) in fruits, vegetables and whole grains helps food move through the body. Water is also very important.

ex.q: Kabir plays football for two hours. What should he eat to get energy quickly, and what helps his muscles grow?
st: Energy comes from carbohydrates and fats.
A roti or a banana gives carbohydrates for energy.
Dal, eggs or paneer give proteins for growth and repair.
ex.a: Carbohydrate foods for energy, and protein foods to help muscles grow.

topics.rl: Look at your lunch box today. Can you find one energy food, one body-building food and one protective food in it?

topics.t: Balanced diet and healthy food habits
topics.h: Eating only aloo paratha every day sounds yummy, but your body would miss many things. What does a happy, healthy plate look like?
p: A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts, along with water and roughage.
Millets like ragi, bajra and jowar are healthy grains grown in India. The year 2023 was celebrated as the International Year of Millets.
Junk food has too much oil, salt or sugar and few useful nutrients. We should eat it only once in a while.
Wash your hands before eating, wash fruits and vegetables, and keep food covered.
Food can be kept from spoiling by keeping it cool, drying it (like papad) or using salt, oil or sugar (like pickles and jam).

ex.q: Riya's lunch is two samosas and a cold drink. Think it through: is it a balanced meal? How can she improve it?
st: Samosas are fried, so they have a lot of fat and carbohydrates.
The cold drink has a lot of sugar.
There is little protein, vitamins or fibre.
She can eat roti with dal, sabzi, salad and a glass of buttermilk instead.
ex.a: It is not balanced. A meal like roti, dal, sabzi, salad and buttermilk is better.

topics.rl: Many government schools serve hot cooked mid-day meals (the PM POSHAN scheme). These meals include grains, dal and vegetables to keep children healthy.

topics.h: Who opens the school gate before you arrive? Who makes the garden bloom? A school runs because many people work together!
p: A school community is all the people who make the school work: students, teachers, the principal, office staff, cleaning staff, the gardener, the guard, cooks and bus drivers.
Each person's work is important, so we respect and thank everyone.
Parents also help. They meet teachers and may be part of the School Management Committee.
Students help too: as class monitors, in the eco-club, by keeping the classroom clean and caring for the school garden.
A good school welcomes everyone. Ramps help wheelchair users, books in Braille help children who cannot see, and sign language helps children who cannot hear.

ex.q: A new girl, Lhamo, uses a wheelchair. Her classroom is on the first floor and there is no ramp or lift. Think it through: what can the school do?
st: Every child has the right to reach the classroom.
A ramp or lift would help her move on her own.
Until then, the class could be moved to the ground floor.
ex.a: Build a ramp or lift, and meanwhile hold her class on the ground floor.

topics.rl: Next time you see the school guard, the cleaning didi or bhaiya, or the gardener, say 'Thank you!' They help make your school a happy place.

topics.h: Have you ever felt happy, nervous and excited all on the same day? Feelings are normal, and a happy school helps everyone feel safe.
p: Everyone has feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared or excited. All feelings are okay. Talking about them helps.
When we feel upset, we can take deep breaths, count to ten, or talk to a friend, parent or teacher.
Being kind means sharing, helping, listening and including others in games.
Bullying means hurting someone again and again with words or actions. It is never okay. Tell a teacher or a trusted adult.
Our body is our own. If any touch makes you feel uncomfortable, say 'No', move away, and tell a trusted adult.

ex.q: At lunch, Samar sees some children laughing at a new boy's accent every day. Think it through: what should Samar do?
st: Laughing at someone again and again is bullying.
Samar can be kind to the new boy and sit with him.
He should tell the class teacher so that the bullying stops.
ex.a: Be kind to the new boy and tell a teacher about the bullying.

topics.rl: Many schools start the day with yoga or a few minutes of quiet breathing. It helps both the body and the mind feel fresh.

topics.h: Fire drills, earthquake drills, first aid boxes: schools practise safety so that everyone knows what to do if something goes wrong.
p: In an earthquake: Drop to the floor, take Cover under a strong desk, and Hold on until the shaking stops.
During a fire drill: stay calm, walk quickly in a line, do not run or push, use the stairs (never the lift), and go to the safe open ground.
For a small cut: wash it with clean water, cover it with a clean bandage, and tell an adult.
On the road: cross at a zebra crossing. Look right, then left, then right again. Red light means stop and green light means go.
In India, 112 is the one number to call for police, fire or ambulance help in an emergency.

ex.q: The fire alarm rings during class. Two children want to run to the lift to get out quickly. Think it through: what should the class do?
st: Lifts can stop working in a fire and trap people.
Running and pushing can make people fall.
So the class should line up, walk quickly down the stairs and go to the open ground.
ex.a: Walk calmly in a line, use the stairs, not the lift, and gather in the open ground.

topics.rl: Find your school's first aid box and the fire extinguisher. Do you know where the assembly point is during a drill?

topics.h: In one train journey across India, you could hear ten languages, taste twenty kinds of rotis and see snow, deserts and beaches. Yet we are all Indians!
p: India has 28 states and 8 union territories. New Delhi is the capital of India.
People in India speak many languages. The Constitution lists 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, including Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and Assamese.
India has snowy mountains, hot deserts, green forests, long coasts and wide plains. So people's food, clothes and homes are different in different places.
People of many faiths live together and enjoy one another's festivals.
We celebrate national festivals together: Republic Day (26 January), Independence Day (15 August) and Gandhi Jayanti (2 October).

ex.q: People in Ladakh wear thick woollen clothes, while people in Kerala wear light cotton. Think it through: why?
st: Ladakh is high in the mountains and is very cold.
Kerala is near the sea and is warm and humid.
People choose clothes that suit the weather of their place.
ex.a: Because the weather is different: cold in Ladakh, warm in Kerala.

topics.rl: Look at a ₹10 note. Its value is written in many Indian languages: a small sign of our unity in diversity.

topics.h: Bihu in Assam, Onam in Kerala, Pongal in Tamil Nadu: every state has its own festivals, dances and tasty food. Let's go on a culture trip!
p: Many festivals are linked to harvests: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Onam in Kerala and Baisakhi in Punjab.
Each state has its own dances: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathakali (Kerala), Bhangra (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Ghoomar (Rajasthan) and Odissi (Odisha).
Each region has special food: dhokla from Gujarat, litti chokha from Bihar, dal baati churma from Rajasthan, and makki di roti with sarson da saag from Punjab.
The Hornbill Festival of Nagaland shows the dances, songs and crafts of the state's many tribes.
Every state has a capital. For example, Dispur is the capital of Assam and Jaipur is the capital of Rajasthan.

ex.q: Neha's family is going to see the boat races during Onam. Which state will they visit?
st: Onam is the harvest festival of Kerala.
Snake-boat races are held on Kerala's backwaters around Onam.
So they will visit Kerala.
ex.a: Kerala.

topics.rl: Next time you eat at a wedding or a food fair, try a dish from another state and find out where it comes from!

topics.h: Fish and peacocks painted in Bihar, stick-figure dancers painted in Maharashtra: Indian art tells stories in many styles!
p: Madhubani paintings come from Bihar. They use bright colours and pictures of fish, birds and nature.
Warli paintings come from Maharashtra. They use white stick figures of people, animals and trees.
Gond paintings come from Madhya Pradesh and are made with lines and dots. Blue pottery is a famous craft of Jaipur in Rajasthan.
Our national symbols unite all Indians: the tiger is our national animal, the peacock our national bird and the lotus our national flower.
The banyan is our national tree and the mango is our national fruit.

ex.q: A painting shows white stick figures dancing in a circle on a brown wall. Think it through: which art form is it?
st: Madhubani uses bright colours and fish and bird designs.
Warli uses simple white stick figures.
So the painting is Warli art.
ex.a: Warli art from Maharashtra.

topics.rl: Look around at a craft fair or museum: you may spot Madhubani, Warli or blue pottery. Each tells the story of the place where it was made.

topics.h: Some deserts burn hot with golden sand. Others are freezing cold with snowy mountains! India has both kinds.
p: A desert is a place that gets very little rain.
The Thar Desert is a hot desert, mostly in Rajasthan. It has sand dunes, very hot days and cool nights. Jaisalmer is a city in the Thar.
Ladakh is a cold desert. It is high in the mountains, gets very little rain, and has freezing winters.
The camel is called the 'ship of the desert'. Its wide, padded feet do not sink in sand, and its hump stores fat, not water. In Ladakh's Nubra Valley there are two-humped camels.
The Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is a huge salt desert. In winter it shines white like snow.

ex.q: Think it through: why do houses in the Thar Desert often have thick mud walls?
st: Days in the desert are very hot.
Thick mud walls do not let heat in quickly.
So the inside of the house stays cooler during the day.
ex.a: Thick mud walls keep the house cool in the hot desert.

topics.rl: Many people visit the Rann Utsav in Kutch in winter and enjoy camel rides on the dunes near Jaisalmer.

topics.h: Imagine a piece of land with sea all around it, coconut trees, and coral reefs full of colourful fish. Welcome to India's islands!
p: An island is land that has water all around it.
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are in the Bay of Bengal. Their capital is Sri Vijaya Puram (earlier called Port Blair).
Lakshadweep is a group of small coral islands in the Arabian Sea. Its capital is Kavaratti.
Corals look like rocks or plants, but they are made by tiny sea animals. Coral reefs are home to many fish.
Barren Island in the Andaman Sea has India's only active volcano. Majuli in Assam is a huge island in the Brahmaputra river.

ex.q: Lakshadweep and the Andaman Islands are both groups of islands. Think it through: how can you tell them apart on a map?
st: Find India's west and east coasts.
Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea, to the west.
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands are in the Bay of Bengal, to the east.
ex.a: Lakshadweep is in the Arabian Sea (west); Andaman and Nicobar are in the Bay of Bengal (east).

topics.rl: Fish, coconut and seafood are a big part of meals on India's islands, and many people work as fishers or in tourism.

topics.h: Bridges made of living tree roots, a lake with floating islands, and the tallest mountains on Earth: India's wonders are real!
p: The Himalayas in the north are the highest mountains in the world. Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, stands on the border of Nepal and China.
Kangchenjunga, on the border of Sikkim and Nepal, is the third-highest peak in the world. You can see it from Sikkim and Darjeeling.
In hills, houses often have sloping roofs so that rain and snow slide off easily.
Mawsynram and Sohra (Cherrapunji) in Meghalaya are among the wettest places on Earth. People there grow living root bridges from the roots of rubber fig trees.
Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating islands called phumdis. The rare sangai deer lives in a floating national park there.

ex.q: Think it through: why do houses in Himachal Pradesh often have sloping roofs, while houses in the Thar Desert often have flat roofs?
st: Himachal gets heavy rain and snow.
Sloping roofs let rain and snow slide off.
The Thar gets very little rain, so a flat roof works well and can be used for sleeping on hot nights.
ex.a: Sloping roofs suit places with lots of rain and snow; flat roofs suit dry places.

topics.rl: On a trip to Shillong, you might cross a living root bridge. On a trip to Darjeeling or Sikkim, you might see snowy Kangchenjunga at sunrise.

topics.t: Forms of energy and how they change
topics.h: A fan spins, a bulb glows, a pressure cooker whistles and you run around the playground. All of this needs energy!
p: Energy is what makes things work, move, grow, light up or heat up.
Energy comes in many forms: heat, light, sound, electrical energy and the energy of moving things.
Energy can be stored. Food, fuels like LPG and wood, and batteries all hold stored (chemical) energy.
Energy changes from one form to another. A fan changes electrical energy into movement. A bulb changes electrical energy into light and some heat.
Our body changes the stored energy of food into movement and body heat.

ex.q: Priya switches on a torch. Think it through: what energy changes happen?
st: The battery has stored (chemical) energy.
It changes into electrical energy that flows through the wire.
The bulb changes electrical energy into light (and a little heat).
ex.a: Stored energy in the battery → electrical energy → light.

topics.rl: Have you noticed that a phone or a laptop gets warm after it has been used for a long time? Some energy always turns into heat!

topics.h: The Sun has been shining for billions of years and gives us light and heat every day for free. What other sources of energy do we use?
p: The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth. Plants use sunlight to make food, and animals eat plants.
Renewable sources do not run out: sunlight, wind, flowing water and biogas.
Non-renewable sources will run out one day: coal, petroleum (from which petrol and diesel are made) and natural gas. They formed deep underground over millions of years.
Burning coal, petrol and diesel makes smoke that pollutes the air.
Biogas is made from cow dung and kitchen waste. Dams use flowing water to make electricity.

ex.q: A village has strong sunshine almost all year. Think it through: which source of electricity would suit it best?
st: Sunlight is free and does not run out.
Solar panels on roofs can turn sunlight into electricity.
They do not make smoke.
ex.a: Solar energy, using solar panels.

topics.rl: You can see big wind turbines on hills and coasts in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, and solar panels on many rooftops and railway stations.

topics.h: If every home in India switched off just one extra light for an hour each day, a huge amount of electricity would be saved!
p: Switch off lights, fans and TVs when you leave a room.
LED bulbs give good light but use much less electricity than old bulbs.
When buying a fridge or AC, look for the star label. More stars means it uses less electricity.
Use sunlight during the day: open the curtains instead of switching on lights.
Walk, cycle or use buses and trains for short trips. Cover pots while cooking and use a pressure cooker to save gas.

ex.q: An old bulb uses 60 watts. An LED bulb gives the same light using 10 watts. How many watts does the LED save?
st: Old bulb: 60 watts
LED bulb: 10 watts
ex.a: 50 watts.

topics.rl: 14 December is National Energy Conservation Day in India. Make a 'Switch-off Squad' in your class to check lights and fans at break time!

topics.h: Your cotton T-shirt grew on a plant, your woollen sweater was once on a sheep, and your raincoat came from petroleum! Clothes have surprising beginnings.
p: Clothes are made of fabric, and fabric is made of thin threads called fibres.
Plant fibres: cotton comes from the fluffy balls (bolls) of the cotton plant, jute from the stem of the jute plant, and coir from coconut husks.
Animal fibres: wool comes from the hair of sheep, goats, yaks and camels. Silk comes from the cocoons made by silkworms.
Synthetic (man-made) fibres like nylon and polyester are made in factories from chemicals that come from petroleum.
Cotton soaks up sweat and is cool for summer. Wool traps air and keeps us warm in winter.

ex.q: Think it through: why is cotton better than nylon for a hot summer day in Chennai?
st: In hot weather we sweat a lot.
Cotton soaks up sweat and lets air pass through.
Nylon does not soak up sweat well, so we feel sticky.
ex.a: Cotton soaks up sweat and keeps us cool.

topics.rl: Jute is called the 'golden fibre'. It is grown a lot in West Bengal and is used to make strong sacks, bags and ropes.

topics.h: A cotton ball and a shirt look nothing alike. How does fluffy cotton become a smart school shirt? Let's follow the steps!
p: Cotton bolls are picked from the plants. Then the seeds are removed from the cotton. This is called ginning.
Fibres are twisted together to make a long thread called yarn. This is spinning. A charkha (spinning wheel) or a takli can spin yarn by hand.
Yarn is woven or knitted into fabric. Fabric is dyed or printed in colours, then cut and stitched into clothes.
For wool, sheep's hair is cut off (shearing, which does not hurt the sheep, like a haircut). It is washed, sorted, combed and spun into yarn.
For silk, silkworms spin cocoons. The fine silk thread is unwound from the cocoons and woven into silk fabric.

ex.q: Mahatma Gandhi spun yarn on a charkha every day. Think it through: what is khadi?
st: Gandhiji wanted Indians to make their own cloth.
Yarn was spun by hand on a charkha.
The yarn was then woven by hand into cloth.
ex.a: Khadi is cloth made from hand-spun and hand-woven yarn.

topics.rl: If you visit a khadi shop, you'll see cloth made by hand-spinning and hand-weaving, just like in Gandhiji's time.

topics.h: Banarasi silk, Kanchipuram sarees, Pochampally ikat: India is famous around the world for its beautiful handmade textiles!
p: Weaving uses two sets of threads crossing each other at right angles on a loom. The long threads are the warp and the threads going across are the weft.
Knitting uses one long yarn made into loops. Sweaters and socks are often knitted.
A handloom is worked by hand and feet. A powerloom runs on electricity.
Famous textiles: Banarasi silk from Varanasi, Kanchipuram silk from Tamil Nadu, Pochampally ikat from Telangana, golden Muga silk from Assam, and Bandhani tie-dye from Gujarat and Rajasthan.
National Handloom Day is on 7 August. Old clothes can be reused as bags, mats or dusters, or given to someone who needs them.

ex.q: Make a mini weave: cut paper strips (ask an adult to help with the scissors) and weave them through slits in a sheet of paper. Think it through: how do the strips go?
st: Fix strips lengthwise: these are like the warp.
Push a new strip across, going over one and under the next: this is the weft.
The next strip starts the other way, under then over.
ex.a: Over-under strips crossing at right angles make a woven pattern, just like on a loom.

topics.rl: Look at a cotton dupatta or a jute bag closely: you can see tiny threads going up-down and side-to-side. That is weaving!

topics.h: Right now, while you are reading this, the ground under you is spinning! That spinning gives us day and night.
p: The Earth is shaped like a ball (a sphere). It spins on an imaginary line called its axis. This spinning is called rotation.
The Earth takes about 24 hours to spin once. That makes one day and one night.
The half of the Earth facing the Sun has day. The half facing away from the Sun has night.
Because the Earth spins from west to east, the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west.
Shadows are long in the morning and evening, and shortest around noon when the Sun is high in the sky.

ex.q: In a dark room, Rahul's teacher shines a torch on a globe and turns it slowly. Think it through: what does this show?
st: The torch is like the Sun.
Only the side of the globe facing the torch is lit: that side has day.
As the globe turns, places move from light to dark: day changes to night.
ex.a: The spinning Earth gives day to the side facing the Sun and night to the other side.

topics.rl: Arunachal Pradesh, in the far east of India, sees the sunrise before Gujarat in the far west. That is because the Earth spins from west to east.

topics.h: Mangoes in summer, rain in the monsoon, warm sweaters in winter: nature repeats its patterns every year like a song with a beat!
p: The Earth goes around the Sun. This is called revolution. One trip takes about 365 days, which is one year.
The Earth's axis is tilted. Because of this tilt, different places get different amounts of sunlight during the year, and we get seasons.
In India we have summer, the monsoon (rainy season), autumn, winter and spring. Traditional Indian calendars name six seasons, called ritus.
The Moon seems to change shape. From one new moon (amavasya) to the next full moon (purnima) takes about 15 days, and the whole cycle takes about a month.
Plants follow cycles too. Many trees shed leaves and grow new ones every year. The Neelakurinji flower of the Western Ghats blooms only once in 12 years!

ex.q: A year usually has 365 days, but almost every fourth year has 366 days. Think it through: why?
st: The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go around the Sun.
Four quarters add up to one whole day.
So every four years, one extra day (29 February) is added.
ex.a: To add up the extra quarter days; that year is a leap year.

topics.rl: Many Indian festivals follow nature's rhythm: Diwali falls on a new moon night, Holi near a full moon, and harvest festivals in spring and winter.

topics.h: Every winter, thousands of birds fly over the Himalayas to visit India, and some come all the way from Central Asia and Siberia. Why do they make such long trips?
p: Migration is when animals travel far from one place to another at a certain time of the year, and later return.
Animals migrate to find food, to escape the cold, or to lay eggs and raise their young.
Amur falcons stop in Nagaland every October–November on their long journey to Africa. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas to spend the winter in India.
Flamingos raise their chicks in the Rann of Kutch. Demoiselle cranes spend winter in Khichan village, Rajasthan.

Olive Ridley sea turtles come in huge numbers to lay eggs on Odisha's beaches. Some herders, like the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh, move with their flocks to the hills in summer and back down in winter.

ex.q: In winter, many lakes in Siberia freeze over. Think it through: why do some birds from there fly to India in winter?
st: Frozen lakes mean birds cannot find fish, insects or plants to eat.
India is warmer in winter, and its lakes and wetlands have food.
So the birds fly to India for the winter and go back in spring.
ex.a: They come to find food and warmth, and go back when the cold ends.

topics.rl: In winter, visit Keoladeo National Park in Bharatpur or Chilika Lake in Odisha to watch migratory birds. Dr Salim Ali, the 'Birdman of India', studied many such birds.

topics.h: A banana peel can turn into soil in a few weeks, but a plastic bottle can stay around for hundreds of years. What happens to the things we throw away?
p: Pollution means making air, water or land dirty and harmful.
Smoke from vehicles, factories and burning garbage pollutes the air. Sewage and waste pollute water. Plastic and garbage pollute land.
Follow the 3 Rs: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (make new things from old ones).
Separate waste at home: wet waste like peels and leftover food goes in the green bin; dry waste like paper, plastic, metal and glass goes in the blue bin.
Wet kitchen waste can be turned into compost, a natural manure for plants. Carry a cloth bag instead of taking plastic bags.

ex.q: After a birthday party, there are banana peels, paper plates, plastic spoons and a glass bottle. Think it through: how should they be sorted?
st: Banana peels rot easily: they are wet waste for the green bin.
Paper plates, plastic spoons and the glass bottle are dry waste for the blue bin.
Even better next time: use steel plates and spoons that can be washed and reused.
ex.a: Peels in the green (wet) bin; paper, plastic and glass in the blue (dry) bin.

topics.rl: Many cities, like Indore, collect wet and dry waste separately from every home. Does your colony's garbage van have two parts?

topics.h: Have you heard grown-ups say 'summers are getting hotter'? Scientists have found that the Earth is slowly warming. What can we do about it?
p: Weather is what the sky and air are like today: sunny, rainy or windy. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years.
Burning coal, petrol and diesel, and cutting down forests, add a lot of carbon dioxide to the air. This gas traps heat, so the Earth is slowly getting warmer.
A warmer Earth means melting glaciers, rising sea levels, more heatwaves, and very heavy rain or long dry spells in some places.
Trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. Forests also give homes to animals and keep the soil in place.
We can help: plant and care for trees, save electricity, walk, cycle or use buses, and waste less.

ex.q: Mumbai is warm and humid all year, while Shimla is cool most of the year. Is this weather or climate? Think it through.
st: Weather changes from day to day.
Here we are talking about what a place is usually like over many years.
That is climate.
ex.a: It is climate: the usual weather of a place over many years.

topics.rl: Many schools have eco-clubs that plant trees, save water and run 'no plastic' days. Each small step helps our shared home.

topics.h: Ordinary people in India have hugged trees, grown whole forests and protected animals. You can be an Earth hero too!
p: In the Chipko movement, which began in 1973 in the hills of present-day Uttarakhand, villagers hugged trees to stop them from being cut. Gaura Devi and the women of Reni village were part of it.
The Bishnoi people of Rajasthan have protected trees and animals like blackbucks for hundreds of years. In 1730, Amrita Devi and many villagers bravely stood up to save khejri trees.
Jadav Payeng, the 'Forest Man of India', planted trees for years and grew a whole forest on a sandbar of the Brahmaputra in Assam.

National parks protect wildlife: Kaziranga (Assam) for the one-horned rhinoceros, Gir (Gujarat) for Asiatic lions, which live in the wild only in Gujarat, and Jim Corbett (Uttarakhand), India's first national park.
World Environment Day is on 5 June and Earth Day is on 22 April.

ex.q: Your colony plans to cut a big old neem tree to make more parking space. Think it through: what could you do?
st: The tree gives shade, oxygen and a home to birds.
Talk to your parents and the colony members about why the tree matters.
Suggest another place for parking, and plant more trees together.
ex.a: Speak up politely with adults, explain the tree's value and suggest other ideas.

topics.rl: On World Environment Day, many schools plant saplings. If you plant one, give it a name and water it every week!

qa.q: What do we call the change of water into water vapour when it is heated?
qa.e: When water is heated, it turns into water vapour and rises into the air. This is evaporation.

qa.q: Tiny water droplets collect high in the sky. What do they form?
qa.e: Millions of tiny droplets of water together make a cloud.

qa.q: Which gives the heat that drives the water cycle?
qa.e: The Sun heats water on Earth so that it evaporates. Without the Sun's heat, the cycle would stop.

qa.q: Ravi takes a cold bottle out of the fridge. Soon tiny drops appear on the outside. Where did they come from?
qa.a: Water vapour in the air cooled on the bottle
qa.e: Air has water vapour in it. It cools when it touches the cold bottle and turns into drops. This is condensation.

qa.q: Rain, snow and hail falling from clouds are all called what?
qa.e: Any water that falls from clouds to the ground is called precipitation.

qa.q: Plants give out water vapour through tiny holes in their leaves. What is this called?
qa.e: Leaves lose water as vapour to the air. This is transpiration, and it adds water to the water cycle.

qa.q: When will a puddle on the road dry fastest?
qa.a: On a hot, sunny and windy day
qa.e: Heat and wind both make water evaporate faster, so a hot, sunny, windy day dries a puddle quickest.

qa.q: Why is the water cycle called a 'cycle'?
qa.a: Water keeps moving round and round between Earth and sky
qa.e: Water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as rain and returns to seas again and again. So it is a cycle.

qa.q: A cactus grows in the dry desert. Does it need water?
qa.a: Yes, it needs a little water to live
qa.e: A cactus stores water in its thick stem and needs very little, but like every living thing it still needs water.

qa.q: Most of the water on Earth is found in
qa.e: Seas and oceans hold most of Earth's water, and that water is salty.

qa.q: Why can't we drink sea water?
qa.e: Sea water has a lot of salt dissolved in it. It is not fit for drinking.

qa.q: Water that is stored under the ground is called
qa.e: Rainwater seeps into the soil and is stored under the ground. It is called groundwater.

qa.q: Which of these takes out groundwater for us to use?
qa.e: Hand pumps, wells and borewells bring up water from under the ground.

qa.q: How does water help our body?
qa.a: It helps digest food and keeps us cool
qa.e: Water helps digestion, keeps our body temperature right and removes waste through sweat and urine.

qa.q: How much of the Earth's surface is covered by water?
qa.e: About three-fourths of the Earth's surface is water. That is why Earth looks blue from space.

qa.q: Which is the best way to make muddy drinking water safer at home?
qa.a: Filter it and then boil it
qa.e: Filtering removes dirt and boiling kills germs, so the water becomes safer to drink.

qa.q: What is rainwater harvesting?
qa.a: Collecting and storing rainwater for later use
qa.e: Rainwater harvesting means catching rainwater, for example from rooftops, and storing it or sending it into the ground.

qa.q: Rani ki Vav, a beautiful old stepwell, is in which state?
qa.e: Rani ki Vav is in Patan, Gujarat. 'Vav' is the Gujarati word for a stepwell.

qa.q: Why did people build kunds in the Thar Desert?
qa.a: To collect and store the little rain that falls
qa.e: The desert gets very little rain, so people built kunds to save every drop for drinking.

qa.q: Which habit saves the most water while bathing?
qa.e: A bucket bath uses a fixed amount of water, so less water is wasted.

qa.q: Water used for washing vegetables can be reused to
qa.e: This water is a little dirty but fine for plants. We should not drink or cook with it.

qa.q: A johad is
qa.a: a small earthen dam that holds rainwater
qa.e: Johads are small mud dams built across slopes to stop and store rainwater. They help water soak into the ground.

qa.q: Rainwater sent into a pit in the ground helps to
qa.e: Water soaking into the ground refills the groundwater, so wells and hand pumps have water later.

qa.q: World Water Day is celebrated every year on
qa.e: World Water Day is on 22 March. It reminds everyone to save and value water.

qa.q: The place where a river begins is called its
qa.e: A river starts at its source, such as a glacier, a spring or a lake.

qa.q: What is a glacier?
qa.a: A huge, slow-moving mass of ice
qa.e: A glacier is a giant river of ice found high in cold mountains. Its melting ice feeds many rivers.

qa.q: Where does a river usually flow the fastest?
qa.a: In the mountains, near its source
qa.e: Mountains have steep slopes, so the water rushes down quickly.

qa.q: A small river that joins a bigger river is called a
qa.e: A tributary brings its water into a bigger main river. The Yamuna is a tributary of the Ganga.

qa.q: The fine, rich soil that a river spreads on its banks is called
qa.e: Rivers carry tiny bits of soil called silt. When floods spread it on the land, the soil becomes good for farming.

qa.q: The place where a river meets the sea is called its
qa.e: A river ends at its mouth, where it pours into a sea or ocean.

qa.q: Why do many rivers that start in the Himalayas have water all year round?
qa.a: They get water from melting snow and glaciers
qa.e: Snow and glaciers melt, especially in summer, so these rivers keep flowing even when there is no rain.

qa.q: Which place is a delta?
qa.a: Land near a river's mouth made of silt, with many branches
qa.e: As the river slows near the sea, it drops its silt. Over many years this builds new land called a delta.

qa.q: The Ganga begins at which glacier?
qa.e: The Ganga starts from the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand.

qa.q: At Devprayag, the Bhagirathi joins which river to become the Ganga?
qa.e: The Bhagirathi and the Alaknanda meet at Devprayag. From there the river is called the Ganga.

qa.q: Which river is a tributary of the Ganga and meets it at Prayagraj?
qa.e: The Yamuna joins the Ganga at Prayagraj. This meeting point is called the Sangam.

qa.q: Into which sea does the Ganga finally flow?
qa.e: The Ganga flows east and enters the Bay of Bengal.

qa.q: Which of these rivers flows west into the Arabian Sea?
qa.e: The Narmada flows from Amarkantak towards the west and enters the Arabian Sea in Gujarat.

qa.q: Majuli, a huge island in the middle of a river, is in which river?
qa.e: Majuli is a river island in the Brahmaputra in Assam.

qa.q: Which animal lives in the Sundarbans delta?
qa.e: The Sundarbans mangrove forest in the Ganga–Brahmaputra delta is home to the Royal Bengal tiger.

qa.q: Where does the Brahmaputra begin?
qa.e: The Brahmaputra starts in Tibet, then enters India through Arunachal Pradesh.

qa.q: Why is land in river plains good for farming?
qa.a: Rivers spread fertile silt on it
qa.e: Silt from rivers is rich in nutrients, so crops grow well in river plains.

qa.q: Which is India's national aquatic animal?
qa.e: The Ganges river dolphin was named India's national aquatic animal in 2009. It lives in rivers, not the sea.

qa.q: What can a dam on a river help to do?
qa.e: Dams hold back river water for farming and drinking, and the falling water can make electricity.

qa.q: Which city stands on the banks of the Brahmaputra?
qa.e: Guwahati in Assam is on the Brahmaputra.

qa.q: Which of these makes a river dirty?
qa.a: Pouring sewage and factory waste into it
qa.e: Sewage and factory waste carry dirt and harmful things into the water.

qa.q: Who depends on a river to earn a living by catching fish?
qa.e: Fisherfolk catch fish from rivers and sell them.

qa.q: Ravi sees a plastic bottle floating in the river at a picnic. What is the best thing to do?
qa.a: Ask an adult to help pick it out safely and put it in a dustbin
qa.e: Plastic harms river animals, but safety comes first: an adult can help remove it safely.

qa.q: Why did many big cities grow along rivers?
qa.a: Rivers gave water, food and an easy way to travel
qa.e: Water for drinking and farming, fish to eat and boats for trade made river banks good places to live.

qa.q: Where does digestion of food begin?
qa.e: Digestion starts in the mouth, where teeth chew food and saliva mixes with it.

qa.q: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
qa.e: The food pipe carries swallowed food down to the stomach. The wind pipe carries air to the lungs.

qa.q: Which teeth are best for grinding food?
qa.e: Molars at the back have broad, flat tops for grinding and crushing.

qa.q: In which part does most of the useful food go into the blood?
qa.e: Digestion is completed in the small intestine, and the useful parts of food pass into the blood there.

qa.q: What does the large intestine mainly take back from leftover food?
qa.e: The large intestine soaks up water from the leftover food. Then the waste leaves the body.

qa.q: Saliva helps digestion because it
qa.a: makes food soft and starts breaking down starch
qa.e: Saliva wets the food so we can swallow it, and starts changing starch into sugar.

qa.q: How many milk teeth does a child usually have?
qa.e: Children usually have 20 milk teeth. Adults have up to 32 permanent teeth.

qa.q: Why should we chew food well before swallowing?
qa.a: Small soft pieces are easier to digest
qa.e: Chewing breaks food into small pieces and mixes it with saliva, so the stomach and intestines can digest it easily.

qa.q: Which nutrient mainly gives us energy?
qa.e: Carbohydrates in rice, roti and potatoes are the body's main energy food.

qa.q: Which food is rich in proteins?
qa.e: Dals and pulses are rich in proteins, which help the body grow and repair itself.

qa.q: Which nutrient helps the body grow and repair itself?
qa.e: Proteins are body-building nutrients. They help us grow and heal.

qa.q: Which mineral in milk keeps bones and teeth strong?
qa.e: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard and strong. Milk, curd and ragi have calcium.

qa.q: What does roughage (fibre) do for us?
qa.a: Helps food and waste move through the body
qa.e: Fibre does not give much energy, but it helps food move smoothly through the intestines.

qa.q: Which fruit is very rich in vitamin C?
qa.e: Amla (Indian gooseberry) has a lot of vitamin C, which helps keep gums and skin healthy.

qa.q: Our body can make vitamin D when our skin gets
qa.e: When sunlight falls on our skin, the body makes vitamin D, which helps keep bones strong.

qa.q: Which of these foods is rich in fats?
qa.e: Butter, ghee, oil and nuts are rich in fats, which also give energy.

qa.q: What is a balanced diet?
qa.a: Food with all nutrients in the right amounts
qa.e: A balanced diet gives the body every nutrient it needs, in the right amounts.

qa.q: Which of these is a millet?
qa.e: Ragi (finger millet) is a millet. Rice and wheat are other grains, and moong is a pulse.

qa.q: The year 2023 was celebrated around the world as the International Year of
qa.e: The United Nations declared 2023 the International Year of Millets, after India proposed it.

qa.q: Why should we eat junk food only once in a while?
qa.a: It has too much oil, salt or sugar and few nutrients
qa.e: Junk food fills us up but gives few useful nutrients, and too much fat, salt or sugar is bad for health.

qa.q: Which meal is the most balanced?
qa.a: Roti, dal, mixed sabzi, salad and curd
qa.e: It has carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and fibre together.

qa.q: How are papads kept from spoiling?
qa.a: They are dried in the sun
qa.e: Drying removes water. Germs that spoil food need water to grow, so dry papads last long.

qa.q: Which is a healthy food habit?
qa.e: Washing fruits removes dirt and germs, keeping us safe.

qa.q: Which is a sign that food has gone bad?
qa.a: It smells bad or has fuzzy mould on it
qa.e: A bad smell, a strange taste or mould means germs have spoilt the food.

qa.q: Which group best describes a school community?
qa.a: Students, teachers, staff and parents together
qa.e: Everyone who helps the school run is part of its community.

qa.q: Who usually looks after the plants in the school garden?
qa.e: The gardener (mali) waters, plants and cares for the school garden.

qa.q: Why should we respect the cleaning staff of our school?
qa.a: Their work keeps the school clean and healthy for all
qa.e: Every job in school is important. A clean school keeps all of us healthy.

qa.q: Braille is a way of reading using
qa.a: raised dots felt with the fingers
qa.e: Braille uses patterns of raised dots. People who cannot see read them with their fingertips.

qa.q: Who invented Braille?
qa.e: Louis Braille of France made this reading system. He had lost his own eyesight as a child.

qa.q: What helps a child who uses a wheelchair enter the school building on their own?
qa.e: A ramp is a gentle slope, so a wheelchair can roll up it.

qa.q: How can students help keep their school a happy place?
qa.a: Keep classrooms clean and be kind to everyone
qa.e: Clean, cared-for classrooms and kind friends make school pleasant for all.

qa.q: The School Management Committee includes
qa.e: Parents, teachers and local members meet to help plan and improve the school.

qa.q: Which of these is a good way to calm down when you feel angry?
qa.e: Slow breathing helps the body relax so we can think clearly.

qa.q: What is bullying?
qa.a: Hurting someone again and again with words or actions
qa.e: Bullying is repeated hurting, teasing or leaving someone out on purpose.

qa.q: If someone is bullying you, what should you do?
qa.a: Tell a teacher or a trusted adult
qa.e: A trusted adult can help stop the bullying. You do not have to handle it alone.

qa.q: A new girl is sitting alone at playtime. What is the kind thing to do?
qa.a: Invite her to join your game
qa.e: Including others helps them feel welcome.

qa.q: Who is a 'trusted adult'?
qa.a: A grown-up you know well who keeps you safe, like a parent or teacher
qa.e: A trusted adult is someone who cares for you, like a parent, grandparent or teacher.

qa.q: Which of these helps keep our body and mind healthy?
qa.a: Playing, enough sleep and healthy food
qa.e: Exercise, sleep and good food keep us fit, fresh and in a good mood.

qa.q: Meera feels nervous before her dance show. What can help her?
qa.a: Talking to her teacher and taking deep breaths
qa.e: Sharing the feeling and breathing slowly can calm nervousness. Feeling nervous is normal.

qa.q: Your friend made a mistake and feels bad. What can you say?
qa.a: It's okay, everyone makes mistakes. Let's try again.
qa.e: Kind words help a friend feel better and try again.

qa.q: What should you do first when an earthquake starts in class?
qa.a: Drop, take cover under a strong desk and hold on
qa.e: Drop, Cover and Hold on protects your head and body from falling things.

qa.q: Why should we NOT use the lift during a fire?
qa.a: It may stop working and trap people
qa.e: Fire can cut the electricity, so a lift may get stuck. Stairs are safer.

qa.q: Which is the right way to cross a road?
qa.a: At the zebra crossing, after looking right, left and right again
qa.e: Zebra crossings are made for walkers, and looking both ways makes sure no vehicle is coming.

qa.q: Which number can you call in India for police, fire or ambulance help?
qa.e: 112 is India's single emergency number for all urgent help.

qa.q: Aditi gets a small scrape on her knee while playing. What should be done first?
qa.a: Wash it with clean water and cover it with a clean bandage
qa.e: Clean water washes away dirt and germs, and a bandage keeps the wound clean.

qa.q: What does a yellow (amber) traffic light usually tell drivers?
qa.e: Amber means the light is about to change, so drivers should slow down and get ready to stop.

qa.q: Why does a school hold fire drills and earthquake drills?
qa.a: So everyone knows what to do and stays calm in a real emergency
qa.e: Practice helps us act quickly and safely without panic.

qa.q: During a fire drill, the class should
qa.a: walk quickly in a line without pushing
qa.e: Walking in a line keeps everyone safe. Bags and toys can be left behind.

qa.q: How many states does India have?
qa.e: India has 28 states. It also has 8 union territories.

qa.q: How many union territories does India have?
qa.e: India has 8 union territories, such as Delhi, Ladakh and Lakshadweep.

qa.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
qa.e: The Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages, from Assamese to Urdu.

qa.q: What does 'unity in diversity' mean?
qa.a: We are different in many ways but stay together as one country
qa.e: Indians have different languages, food and festivals, but we are united as one nation.

qa.q: We celebrate Republic Day on
qa.e: Our Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, so we celebrate Republic Day on that date.

qa.q: Who wrote India's national anthem, 'Jana Gana Mana'?
qa.e: Rabindranath Tagore wrote 'Jana Gana Mana'. Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote the national song 'Vande Mataram'.

qa.q: Why do people in different parts of India eat different foods?
qa.a: Different crops grow in different climates and soils
qa.e: Rice grows well in wet places and wheat in drier places, so local food depends on what grows nearby.

qa.q: What is the capital of India?
qa.e: New Delhi is the capital. Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai are large cities and state capitals.

qa.q: Bihu is a festival of which state?
qa.e: Bihu is celebrated in Assam with music, dance and feasts.

qa.q: Which dance form comes from Tamil Nadu?
qa.e: Bharatanatyam is a classical dance from Tamil Nadu.

qa.q: Garba is a popular dance of
qa.e: Garba is danced in circles in Gujarat, especially during Navratri.

qa.q: Dhokla is a well-known snack from
qa.e: Dhokla is a soft, steamed snack made from gram flour in Gujarat.

qa.q: Litti chokha is a famous dish of
qa.e: Litti chokha, baked wheat balls stuffed with sattu, is loved in Bihar.

qa.q: Kathakali, a dance with colourful face paint, belongs to which state?
qa.e: Kathakali comes from Kerala. Dancers wear bright make-up and big costumes.

qa.q: What is the capital of Rajasthan?
qa.e: Jaipur, the Pink City, is the capital of Rajasthan. The other options are cities in Rajasthan too, but not the capital.

qa.q: Pongal, Bihu, Onam and Baisakhi are all festivals linked to
qa.e: These festivals celebrate the harvest of crops and thank nature.

qa.q: Madhubani paintings come from which state?
qa.e: Madhubani art comes from the Mithila region of Bihar.

qa.q: Which art uses simple white stick figures?
qa.e: Warli artists of Maharashtra draw people and animals with circles, triangles and lines in white.

qa.q: What is India's national animal?
qa.e: The tiger is India's national animal. The elephant is our national heritage animal.

qa.q: What is India's national bird?
qa.e: The peacock, with its colourful tail feathers, is India's national bird.

qa.q: Which is India's national flower?
qa.e: The lotus grows in water and is India's national flower.

qa.q: Blue pottery is a famous craft of which city?
qa.e: Jaipur in Rajasthan is known for its blue pottery with flower and bird designs.

qa.q: Gond art, made with lines and dots, comes from
qa.e: Gond paintings are made by Gond artists in Madhya Pradesh.

qa.q: Which of these is India's national tree?
qa.e: The banyan tree, with roots hanging from its branches, is India's national tree.

qa.q: What makes a place a desert?
qa.e: Deserts are dry because they get very little rain. They can be hot or cold.

qa.q: The Thar Desert is mostly in which state?
qa.e: Most of the Thar Desert lies in western Rajasthan.

qa.q: Why is Ladakh called a cold desert?
qa.a: It is very cold and gets very little rain
qa.e: Ladakh is high in the mountains, so it is cold, and it gets very little rain.

qa.q: What does a camel's hump store?
qa.e: The hump stores fat, which the camel can use for energy when food is scarce.

qa.q: How do a camel's feet help it walk on sand?
qa.a: They are wide and padded, so they don't sink
qa.e: Wide, padded feet spread the camel's weight, so it does not sink into soft sand.

qa.q: Which place is a white salt desert?
qa.e: The Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is covered with a crust of white salt.

qa.q: Which animal helps people carry loads in the cold desert of Ladakh?
qa.e: Yaks have long, thick hair and can live in Ladakh's freezing cold.

qa.q: Jaisalmer, the 'Golden City', is in which desert?
qa.e: Jaisalmer in Rajasthan stands in the Thar Desert. Its yellow sandstone buildings glow golden.

qa.q: What is an island?
qa.a: Land with water all around it
qa.e: An island has water on all sides, like the Andaman Islands in the sea.

qa.q: In which sea are the Andaman and Nicobar Islands?
qa.e: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the Bay of Bengal, east of mainland India.

qa.q: Lakshadweep islands lie in the
qa.e: Lakshadweep is off the coast of Kerala in the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: Corals are made by
qa.e: Corals are built by tiny sea animals. Their hard skeletons form reefs over many years.

qa.q: India's only active volcano is on
qa.e: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea has India's only active volcano.

qa.q: What is the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands now called?
qa.e: In 2024, Port Blair was renamed Sri Vijaya Puram.

qa.q: Majuli is special because it is
qa.a: a large island in a river
qa.e: Majuli sits in the middle of the Brahmaputra river in Assam.

qa.q: Which tree is very common on India's sea islands?
qa.e: Coconut palms grow well in warm, sandy coastal places like Lakshadweep and the Andamans.

qa.q: Which is the highest peak in the world?
qa.e: Mount Everest, about 8,849 m tall, is the highest peak on Earth. It stands on the border of Nepal and China.

qa.q: Kangchenjunga, the third-highest peak in the world, is in which Indian state?
qa.e: Kangchenjunga stands on the border of Sikkim and Nepal. Only Everest and K2 are higher.

qa.q: What are the floating islands of Loktak Lake called?
qa.e: Phumdis are floating masses of plants and soil on Loktak Lake in Manipur.

qa.q: Living root bridges are found in
qa.e: People in Meghalaya guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams to grow strong living bridges.

qa.q: Mawsynram in Meghalaya is famous for
qa.a: getting a huge amount of rain
qa.e: Mawsynram is one of the wettest places on Earth.

qa.q: Why do houses in snowy hills have sloping roofs?
qa.a: So that snow and rain slide off
qa.e: A sloping roof lets heavy snow and rain slide down instead of piling up.

qa.q: The sangai, a rare deer, lives in which state?
qa.e: The sangai lives in Keibul Lamjao National Park on Loktak Lake, Manipur.

qa.q: The Himalayas are in which part of India?
qa.e: The Himalayas stretch across the north of India, from Ladakh to Arunachal Pradesh.

qa.q: Which of these gives our body energy?
qa.e: Food has stored energy. Our body uses it to move, grow and keep warm.

qa.q: An electric fan changes electrical energy mainly into
qa.e: The fan's blades move. So electrical energy becomes energy of movement.

qa.q: A solar panel changes
qa.e: Solar panels catch sunlight and turn it into electricity.

qa.q: Which of these stores energy?
qa.e: A battery stores chemical energy that can become electrical energy.

qa.q: A loudspeaker changes electrical energy into
qa.e: A loudspeaker turns electricity into sound we can hear.

qa.q: When you rub your palms together fast, they get warm. Which form of energy is made?
qa.e: Rubbing changes the energy of movement into heat.

qa.q: What happens to energy in a bulb besides making light?
qa.e: A bulb changes most of the electrical energy into light, and some into heat. That is why bulbs get warm.

qa.q: Which is an example of energy of movement?
qa.e: Anything that moves, like a rolling ball, has energy of movement.

qa.q: What is the main source of energy on Earth?
qa.e: The Sun gives light and heat. Plants use sunlight to make food, which passes on to animals.

qa.q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
qa.e: Wind keeps blowing and will not run out, so it is renewable.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-renewable source of energy?
qa.e: Coal took millions of years to form underground. Once used up, it cannot be replaced quickly.

qa.q: Biogas is made from
qa.e: When cow dung and food waste rot inside a closed tank, they give out biogas for cooking.

qa.q: What is a problem with burning coal and petrol?
qa.a: They make smoke that pollutes the air
qa.e: Burning these fuels releases smoke and harmful gases into the air.

qa.q: How do dams help us get electricity?
qa.a: Flowing water turns machines that make electricity
qa.e: Water from a dam rushes down and turns turbines, which make electricity.

qa.q: Solar panels get their energy from
qa.e: Solar panels change sunlight into electricity.

qa.q: Why should we use more renewable energy?
qa.a: It will not run out and causes less pollution
qa.e: Renewable sources like sun and wind last forever and make little or no smoke.

qa.q: Which bulb uses the least electricity for the same light?
qa.e: LED bulbs give the same light with much less electricity.

qa.q: An old bulb uses 60 watts and an LED bulb uses 10 watts. How many fewer watts does the LED use?
qa.e: 60 − 10 = 50. So the LED uses 50 watts less.

qa.q: Two fridges of the same size: one has 5 stars on its label and one has 2 stars. Which uses less electricity?
qa.e: More stars on the energy label means the appliance uses less electricity.

qa.q: What should you do when you leave your room?
qa.a: Switch off the lights and fan
qa.e: Switching off saves electricity when nobody is using the room.

qa.q: How does covering a pot while cooking help?
qa.a: Food cooks faster and less gas is used
qa.e: A lid keeps the heat inside, so food cooks faster with less fuel.

qa.q: Which way of going to a nearby shop saves fuel?
qa.e: Walking and cycling use no fuel and keep us fit too.

qa.q: In the daytime, the best way to light up a classroom is to
qa.a: open the windows and curtains to let sunlight in
qa.e: Sunlight is free light. Using it saves electricity.

qa.q: National Energy Conservation Day in India is on
qa.e: India marks National Energy Conservation Day on 14 December to remind everyone to save energy.

qa.q: Cotton fibre comes from
qa.a: the bolls of the cotton plant
qa.e: Cotton grows as soft fluffy fibre in the bolls (seed pods) of the cotton plant.

qa.q: Which fibre comes from an animal?
qa.e: Silk comes from the cocoons spun by silkworms.

qa.q: Jute is often called the
qa.e: Jute fibres are shiny and golden-brown, so jute is called the golden fibre.

qa.q: What do silkworms eat?
qa.e: Silkworms feed on mulberry leaves before spinning their cocoons.

qa.q: Nylon and polyester are
qa.e: They are man-made fibres prepared from chemicals that come from petroleum.

qa.q: Coir, used for doormats and ropes, comes from
qa.e: Coir is the rough fibre from the outer husk of coconuts. Kerala makes a lot of coir.

qa.q: Which fabric is best to keep you warm in a Shimla winter?
qa.e: Wool fibres trap air, and trapped air keeps body heat in.

qa.q: Pashmina wool comes from
qa.e: Pashmina comes from the soft under-hair of Changthangi goats that live in the cold of Ladakh.

qa.q: What is ginning?
qa.e: In ginning, the cotton fibres are separated from the seeds.

qa.q: Making yarn by twisting fibres together is called
qa.e: Spinning twists short fibres into a long, strong thread called yarn.

qa.q: Which comes first in making a cotton shirt?
qa.e: First the cotton is picked; ginning, spinning, weaving, dyeing and stitching come later.

qa.q: What is shearing?
qa.a: Cutting the woolly hair off a sheep
qa.e: Shearing is like a haircut for sheep. It does not hurt them, and the wool grows back.

qa.q: After shearing, why is wool washed before spinning?
qa.a: To remove dirt, dust and grease
qa.e: Raw wool has dirt and grease. Washing cleans it before it is combed and spun.

qa.q: Khadi is cloth that is
qa.e: Khadi is made from yarn spun by hand on a charkha and woven by hand.

qa.q: Silk thread is taken from the silkworm's
qa.e: Silkworms spin cocoons of fine silk thread, which is unwound to make silk.

qa.q: Which tool can be used to spin yarn by hand?
qa.e: A takli is a small hand spindle used for spinning yarn. A charkha is a spinning wheel.

qa.q: In weaving, at what angle do the warp and weft threads cross?
qa.e: Warp and weft cross at right angles, which is 90°.

qa.q: The machine on which fabric is woven is called a
qa.e: Fabric is woven on a loom. A charkha and a takli are for spinning yarn.

qa.q: Sweaters and socks are usually made by
qa.e: Knitting makes loops from a single yarn, which gives stretchy fabric for sweaters and socks.

qa.q: Banarasi silk sarees are made in
qa.e: Banaras is another name for Varanasi, so its silk is called Banarasi silk.

qa.q: Golden Muga silk comes from
qa.e: Muga silk, with its natural golden shine, is made in Assam.

qa.q: Bandhani is made by
qa.a: tying small bits of cloth tightly and then dyeing it
qa.e: The tied parts don't take colour, so they make dotted patterns.

qa.q: When is National Handloom Day celebrated?
qa.e: India celebrates National Handloom Day on 7 August to honour handloom weavers.

qa.q: What is a good way to use old clothes that no longer fit?
qa.a: Give them to someone who needs them or make bags and dusters
qa.e: Reusing and donating clothes reduces waste and helps others.

qa.q: Why do we have day and night?
qa.a: The Earth spins on its axis
qa.e: As the Earth spins, each place turns towards the Sun (day) and then away from it (night).

qa.q: How long does the Earth take to spin once on its axis?
qa.e: One spin takes about 24 hours, which is one day and one night together.

qa.q: The spinning of the Earth on its axis is called
qa.e: Spinning on the axis is rotation. Going around the Sun is revolution.

qa.q: In which direction does the Sun rise?
qa.e: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, because the Earth spins from west to east.

qa.q: When is your shadow the shortest on a sunny day?
qa.e: At noon the Sun is high overhead, so shadows are short.

qa.q: What shape is the Earth?
qa.e: The Earth is round like a ball. Photos from space show this.

qa.q: Which part of India sees the sunrise first?
qa.e: The Earth spins from west to east, so places in the east turn towards the Sun first.

qa.q: When it is noon in India, what is it like on the opposite side of the Earth?
qa.e: The side of the Earth facing away from the Sun has night.

qa.q: About how many days does the Earth take to go around the Sun once?
qa.e: One trip around the Sun takes about 365 days (365 and a quarter), which is one year.

qa.q: The Earth moving around the Sun is called
qa.e: Going around the Sun is revolution. Spinning on the axis is rotation.

qa.q: Why do we have seasons?
qa.a: The Earth's axis is tilted as it goes around the Sun
qa.e: Because of the tilt, each place gets more sunlight at some times of the year and less at others.

qa.q: How many days are there in a leap year?
qa.e: A leap year has one extra day, 29 February, so it has 366 days.

qa.q: How often does the Neelakurinji flower bloom?
qa.e: Neelakurinji covers the hills of the Western Ghats in blue only once in 12 years.

qa.q: The night when we cannot see the Moon at all is called
qa.e: On a new moon night the Moon's lit side faces away from us, so we cannot see it.

qa.q: Which season in India brings most of the year's rain?
qa.e: The monsoon brings most of India's rain, mostly from June to September.

qa.q: Which ritu is the season of spring?
qa.e: Vasant ritu is spring. Shishir is winter, Varsha is the rains and Grishma is summer.

qa.q: What is migration?
qa.a: Animals travelling far at a certain time of year and returning later
qa.e: Migration is a long seasonal journey from one place to another and back.

qa.q: Why do many birds migrate to India in winter?
qa.a: To find food and escape the cold
qa.e: Their homes become very cold with little food, while India is warmer and has food.

qa.q: Amur falcons stop in which Indian state on their way to Africa?
qa.e: Huge flocks of Amur falcons rest in Nagaland in October and November.

qa.q: Olive Ridley turtles come to the beaches of Odisha to
qa.e: Thousands of these sea turtles crawl onto the beach to lay eggs in the sand.

qa.q: Khichan village in Rajasthan is famous for its winter visitors, the
qa.e: Thousands of demoiselle cranes spend winter at Khichan, where villagers feed them grain.

qa.q: Which birds fly over the high Himalayas to reach India for winter?
qa.e: Bar-headed geese are among the highest-flying birds and cross the Himalayas.

qa.q: Gaddi herders of Himachal Pradesh take their sheep and goats up to the high hills in
qa.e: In summer the high hills have fresh grass. In winter, when snow falls, the herders come down.

qa.q: Who is known as the 'Birdman of India'?
qa.e: Dr Salim Ali spent his life studying and protecting India's birds.

qa.q: Which of these is wet waste?
qa.e: Vegetable peels rot easily, so they are wet waste for the green bin.

qa.q: Which bin should a plastic bottle go into?
qa.e: Plastic is dry waste. It goes into the blue bin so it can be recycled.

qa.q: What does 'Reuse' mean?
qa.a: Using something again instead of throwing it away
qa.e: Reusing, like using a jam jar as a pencil holder, means less waste.

qa.q: Making new paper from old newspapers is an example of
qa.e: Recycling turns old things into new materials.

qa.q: Which of these causes air pollution?
qa.e: Burning garbage gives out smoke and harmful gases.

qa.q: What is compost?
qa.a: Natural manure made from rotting kitchen and garden waste
qa.e: Peels and leaves rot into dark, rich compost that helps plants grow.

qa.q: Which is the best choice when you go shopping?
qa.a: Carry a cloth bag from home
qa.e: A cloth bag can be used again and again, so we reduce plastic waste.

qa.q: Class 5 collects 6 old bottles every day for 5 days to send for recycling. How many bottles in all?
qa.e: 6 bottles each day for 5 days is 6 × 5 = 30 bottles.

qa.q: What is climate?
qa.a: The usual weather of a place over many years
qa.e: Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a place.

qa.q: 'It is very foggy in Delhi this morning.' This tells us about the
qa.e: It describes one morning, so it is about the weather.

qa.q: Which gas, added by burning fuels, traps heat and warms the Earth?
qa.e: Burning coal, petrol and diesel adds carbon dioxide, which traps heat.

qa.q: Which is a result of the Earth getting warmer?
qa.e: Higher temperatures make glaciers melt and sea levels rise.

qa.q: How do trees help fight the warming of the Earth?
qa.a: They take in carbon dioxide from the air
qa.e: Trees use carbon dioxide to make their food, so they remove some of it from the air.

qa.q: Which action helps protect our climate?
qa.a: Switching off lights when not needed
qa.e: Saving electricity means less coal is burnt in power plants, so less carbon dioxide.

qa.q: A heatwave is
qa.a: a long spell of very hot weather
qa.e: A heatwave means many days of unusually hot weather. Drink water and stay in the shade.

qa.q: Which way of going to school puts the least smoke into the air?
qa.e: Walking and cycling burn no fuel at all.

qa.q: In the Chipko movement, people
qa.a: hugged trees to stop them from being cut
qa.e: 'Chipko' means 'to cling' or 'to hug'. Villagers hugged trees to protect them.

qa.q: The Chipko movement began in the hills of which present-day state?
qa.e: It began in 1973 in the Garhwal hills, now part of Uttarakhand.

qa.q: Which community of Rajasthan is famous for protecting trees and blackbucks?
qa.e: The Bishnois have cared for khejri trees and animals like blackbucks for centuries.

qa.q: Gir National Park in Gujarat is famous for the
qa.e: Asiatic lions live in the wild only in Gujarat, in and around Gir.

qa.q: Kaziranga National Park in Assam is famous for the
qa.e: Kaziranga has the largest number of one-horned rhinos in the world.

qa.q: Who is known as the 'Forest Man of India'?
qa.e: Jadav Payeng planted trees for many years and grew a forest on a sandbar of the Brahmaputra.

qa.q: World Environment Day is celebrated on
qa.e: World Environment Day is on 5 June. 22 April is Earth Day and 22 March is World Water Day.

qa.q: Which is India's first national park?
qa.e: Jim Corbett National Park in Uttarakhand was set up in 1936 and is India's first national park.
